newsitem.title: UK: European debt futures leap up as US payrolls dive.
newsitem.headline: European debt futures leap up as US payrolls dive.

text.p: European debt futures scrambled up on Friday after a stunning drop in U.S. non-farm payrolls in September sent T-bonds shooting over a point higher. "It was massively lower than expected, the markets have taken a massive leap to the upside," said Mark Bays a futures broker for MeesPierson on London's LIFFE floor.
U.S. non-farm payrolls fell 40,000 in September compared with a forecast rise of 166,000 and versus 250,000 in August.
The unemployment rate stood at 5.2 percent, in line with market forecasts and versus 5.1 percent in August.
U.S. T-bond futures rose over a point on the data, taking European debt futures with them.
Core December Bund futures had climbed to 99.44, up 30 basis points on the day by 1239 GMT, from 99.20 prior to the data.
By 1240 GMT, December gilts were up 21/32 at 110-18, compared with 110-02 just before the data were released.

The same sort of jump was seen in December notionnel futures which were at 125.68, up 26 basis points compared with 125.46 previously, while Italian December BTPs leapt 123.32, up 27 basis points on the day.
BTPs had been trading at 123.15 before the payrolls data.
Global debt markets were keenly focused on the September jobs report -- seeking confirmation of the Federal Reserve's decision not to raise U.S. interest rates at its last policy-setting meeting.
Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets said European bonds had latched on to the enthusiasm shown by the U.S. market, but said there were disturbing elements within the report.
"The markets have been caught up by the drop in payrolls. They are rather overlooking the strength of the household survey and the 0.6 percent rise in average earnings," she said.

Lifton said overtime work figures were not particularly weak either. Overtime hours came in at 4.5 versus a revised August figure of 4.5, from 4.4 previously. "The market has not paid as much attention as they perhaps should to other elements in the data."
While the data had given new impetus to view that U.S. economy was slowing, proof of this would really only be reflected in future monthly data, she said.
